children.value: Naive Bayes applies Bayes’ rule with the assumption that the features are independent given the class. The decision sums the log prior and the log likelihoods of the features, learning reduces to counting, and Laplace smoothing keeps unseen values from vetoing a class. Its decisions are often right even though its probabilities are too extreme.

A decision tree classifies with a sequence of tests on single features. ID3 chooses the test with the largest information gain, C4.5 adds thresholds for continuous features and the gain ratio against features with many values, and pruning on a validation set keeps the tree from overfitting.

Single trees have a high variance. Random forests average many randomized trees; gradient boosting adds small trees one at a time, each fitted to the negative gradient of the loss (for the squared error, the residuals of the current ensemble) and added as a correction, and is among the most accurate methods for tabular data, including the learning-to-rank models of web search.

Logistic regression models the log-odds as a linear function and is trained with the cross-entropy loss; its gradient is the prediction minus the target, times the input. It is the discriminative counterpart of Naive Bayes.

children.value: . The kernel trick computes dot products in a high-dimensional feature space without ever constructing it.

k-means minimizes the within-cluster sum of squares with Lloyd’s algorithm and finds a local optimum that depends on the initialization; k-means++ chooses good starting centroids. Expectation maximization fits Gaussian mixtures with soft assignments, and k-means is its hard-assignment special case.
The number of clusters is a capacity parameter: the elbow method and the silhouette score choose it without labels.
